children.translated_text: Mounted upon the excellent grace of <s>Śrī</s>, the beloved of <s>Tripurā</s> is victorious;
the lord, made of eternal bliss, the guru, <s>Nārāyaṇa</s> himself.
With its four sections on implements, metals, the operations of mercury, and treatment,
this <s>Rasakāmadhenu</s>, compiled by <s>Cūḍāmaṇi</s>, is victorious.
Rasas, uparasas, and metals; a mortar-stone and pestle;
earthen instruments, a blowing tube, and an iron apparatus;

children.text: koṣṭhikā vakranālaṃ ca gomayaṃ sāram indhanam
children.translated_text: a furnace, a curved tube, cow-dung, hardwood essence as fuel;
tongs, flat tongs, an earthen vessel, and an iron bowl;
weights, a balance, a cutter, and a touchstone;
a bamboo tube, an iron tube, pestles and mortars;

children.text: mūṣā nāḍyas tathauṣadhyo vasanaṃ kāñjikaṃ viḍam
children.translated_text: crucibles, tubes, and also medicines, cloth, sour gruel, and viḍa salt;
oily substances, acids, salts, alkalis, poisons, and secondary poisons:
having thus collected the equipment, one should undertake the practical operation.
There, the rasas are substances such as cinnabar, mica, sasyaka, and capala, and also gems.
The uparasas are substances such as sulphur, orpiment, and realgar.
The metals are the metallic substances beginning with gold.
Their ashes, essences, and liquids are extremely useful for the incineration and digestion of blessed <s>Rasendra</s>.
Therefore they are explained at the very outset.

children.text: utsedhena navāṅgulaṃ śaśikalāsaṃkhyāṅgulaṃ dairghyato vistāreṇa navāṅgulaṃ rasamitair nimnaṃ tathaivāṅgulaiḥ
children.translated_text: Nine aṅgulas in height, in length as many aṅgulas as the number of the lunar digits, nine aṅgulas in breadth, and likewise as many aṅgulas deep as the number of rasas;

children.text: kaṇṭhe dvyaṅgulasaṃmitaṃ sumasṛṇaṃ droṇārdhayantropamaṃ gharṣaṃ caiva daśāṅgulaṃ talam idaṃ khalvākhyayantraṃ vadet ||
children.translated_text: at the neck measuring two aṅgulas, very smooth, resembling a half-droṇa apparatus, and with a grinding surface of ten aṅgulas: this lower part is called the instrument named khalva.

children.text: utsedhena daśāṅgulaḥ khalu kalātulyāṅgulāyāmavān vistāreṇa daśāṅgulo munimitair nimnas tathārdhāṅgulaiḥ
children.translated_text: Ten aṅgulas in height, truly as long in aṅgulas as the lunar digits, ten aṅgulas in breadth, and, according to the number of sages, half-aṅgulas deep;

children.text: pālyāṃ dvyaṅgulavistṛtaśca masṛṇo 'tīvārdhacandropamo gharṣo dvādaśakāṅgulaśca kathitaḥ khalvottamaḥ siddhaye ||
children.translated_text: on the rim two aṅgulas broad, smooth, very much like a half-moon, and with a grinding surface said to be twelve aṅgulas: this is the best khalva for success.
It may be made of clay, iron, stone, or lodestone;

children.text: anyatra tu kṛtaḥ kāntāyase khalve bhavet koṭiguṇo rasaḥ ||
children.translated_text: but elsewhere, if made as a khalva of magnetic iron, the rasa becomes ten million times more potent.
In this, five palas of mercury should be ground for purification.
In other mortars too one should apply it according to the suitability of each case.
A round khalva should be twelve aṅgulas wide;
it should be four aṅgulas deep, and the pestle eight aṅgulas long.

children.text: lohair nivartito yastu taptakhalvaḥ sa ucyate
children.translated_text: The one that is fashioned from metals is called a heated mortar.
One should kindle a fire of goat dung and chaff and place it on the ground.

children.text: tasyopari sthitaḥ khalvas taptakhalvaḥ sa ucyate
children.translated_text: The khalva placed upon it is called a heated khalva.
A very firm pestle should be made, with a four-aṅgula tip.
It may be made of all metals, of stone, or of lodestone.
An iron one is nine aṅgulas high and six aṅgulas in depth.
With a pestle of eight aṅgulas, this too is called a heated khalva.
In a four-footed iron mortar there is also a base of ten aṅgulas.
Another firm mortar should be made: a stone slab together with a lump of clay;
and an earthen potsherd, variously made from a vessel, iron, udumbara wood, or clay.
The khalva apparatus is said to be threefold for operations such as grinding:
one of stone, one produced from wood, and the third produced from iron.

children.text: lauho navāṅgulaḥ khalvo nimnatve ca ṣaḍaṅgulaḥ
children.translated_text: An iron khalva is nine aṅgulas high and six aṅgulas in depth;
with a pestle of eight aṅgulas, this also has the name heated khalla.
Having made a hearth in the shape of a khalla and filled it with charcoal,

children.text: tasyāṃ niveśya taṃ khallaṃ pārśve bhastrikayā dhamet
children.translated_text: one should set that khalla in it and blow at the side with bellows.
The paste ground inside it, combined with alkalis and acids,
melts with great speed when heated; there is no doubt about this.

children.text: kṛtaḥ kāntāyasā so 'yaṃ bhavet koṭiguṇo rasaḥ ||
children.translated_text: If this is made of magnetic iron, the rasa becomes ten million times more potent.
One should put together goat dung, chaff, and fire into a pit in the ground;
the khalla placed over that is known as the heated khalla.
When a vessel, half of its belly filled with a liquid substance,

children.text: mukhe tiryakkṛte daṇḍe rasaṃ sūtreṇa lambitam ||
children.translated_text: has a rod placed crosswise at its mouth, with the rasa suspended from it by a cord,
one should steam it without touching the bottom; this is known as the dolāyantra.
When a vessel, half of its belly filled with a liquid substance,
has two openings carefully made on both sides of its neck,
one should place a rod through them and, in its middle, a packet of rasa.

children.text: baddhvā tu svedayedevaṃ dolāyantram iti smṛtam ||
children.translated_text: Having tied it, one should steam it in this way; this is known as the dolāyantra.
When a vessel, half of its belly filled with water or liquid,
has two openings carefully made on both sides of its mouth,
one should insert a rod through them and, in its middle, a packet of rasa.

children.text: baddhvā tu svedayedetad dolāyantram iti smṛtam ||
children.translated_text: Having tied it, one should steam this; it is known as the dolāyantra.
After tying medicinal mercury, wrapped in birch bark and in three layers of cloth,

children.text: rasapoṭalikāṃ kāṣṭhe dṛḍhaṃ baddhvā guṇena hi ||
children.translated_text: one should fasten the mercury packet firmly to a piece of wood with a cord.
It should hang and remain suspended inside a jar filled with a fermenting liquid;
below it one should light the fire according to the procedure prescribed for each case.
This is called the dolāyantra.
Mercury and the like, which are to be steamed, should be placed in three layers of cloth.
After sealing it with paste, one should make a tight packet.
In a vessel half-filled in its belly with liquids, on both sides of its mouth,
one should make two holes and then insert a rod there.
In the middle of the rod one should tie the packet of substance very firmly.
Following the path shown by the guru, one should kindle the fire below.
And then one should steam this; it is remembered as the dolā apparatus.
It is especially employed for the purification and similar operations of substances.
Taking the kiṃnara apparatus, one should smear its base with the medicine.
Mercury placed in navasāra should be set in the middle of the apparatus.

children.text: rasopari śarāvaṃ ca saṃdhilepaṃ dṛḍhaṃ mṛdā
children.translated_text: Above the mercury one should place a saucer, and make a firm joint-seal with clay.

children.text: lavaṇena ca sampūrya dvāraṃ saṃrudhya yatnataḥ ||
children.translated_text: Having filled it with salt and carefully closed the opening,
one should set it on a stove and kindle a lamp-like fire beneath.
After one yāma one should take it down, and the mercury should be cooled.

children.text: kṛtvā mṛnmayabhāṇḍasampuṭam adhaḥ prakṣipya bhāṇḍodare turyāṃśārkakarair manāk sakarakaiḥ saṃmardya piṇḍīkṛtam
children.translated_text: Having made a clay-vessel enclosure, putting it below inside the vessel, and gently triturating it with a fourth part of arka-juice and with a little sugar, one should form it into a lump.

children.text: anyasminnicitordhvavāriṇi mṛdā saṃrudhya saṃdhau sudhīḥ paktvā dvipraharaṃ samena śucinā bhāṇḍe tam ūrdhvaṃ nayet ||
children.translated_text: In another vessel, packed with embers and with water above, the wise man should close the joint with clay, cook it for two praharas with an even, clean fire, and cause it to rise upward in the vessel.
Because this same procedure involves setting up a vessel-enclosure, it is the apparatus called ḍamaruka.

children.text: bhūmau hastamitaṃ nimnaṃ vidadhyād gartam uttamam
children.translated_text: One should make an excellent pit in the ground, one hasta deep.

children.text: tasmin pātraṃ nidhāyātha tadrūpaṃ pātram anyakam ||
children.translated_text: After placing a vessel in it, one should take another vessel of the same form.
Then, in that second vessel, one should place the medicines.
Its mouth should be closed with a saucer that has a hole in its center.

children.text: pātram etattu gartasthe pātre yatnena vinyaset
children.translated_text: This vessel should be carefully placed into the vessel set in the pit.
One should carefully make a very firm sealing of the joint between the two.

children.text: mṛdā sampūrya gartaṃ tu vahniṃ dadyāt prayogavit
children.translated_text: The expert in procedure should fill the pit with clay and apply fire.
Then, when the skilled practitioner of <s>rasatantra</s> knows that it has cooled by itself,

children.text: uparisthaṃ tu vai pātraṃ śanaiḥ samavatārayet
children.translated_text: he should slowly take down the vessel placed above.
He should then collect, according to rule, the oil that has gone into the lower vessel.
This has been named by the learned the apparatus called pātāla.
It is used to obtain the oil of sulfur and the like.
One should cook a kumudī vessel set in a pit, its whole body packed with sand,
and cover it with blazing cow-dung cakes; the apparatus is called bhūdhara.
A crucible containing mercury, with its whole body hidden in sand in a pit,
should be covered with blazing cow-dung cakes; that apparatus is called bhūdhara.
Or, having made the apparatus like a ḍamaru, or like a downward distillation apparatus,
one should bury it in a pit in the ground and heap fire above it.

children.text: adhaḥsthālyāṃ jalaṃ kṣiptvā sūtakaṃ tatra pātayet
children.translated_text: Putting water in the lower pot, one should cause the mercury to descend there.
This is the bhūdhara apparatus in the operation for processing mercury.
Having placed one pot upon another pot in an inverted position,
one should cook this in due order; the apparatus is called ḍamaruka.
In a jar set on a stove one should place water and the like.

children.text: adhomukhaṃ ghaṭaṃ tv anyaṃ mukhe tasya nidhāpayet ||
children.translated_text: Another jar, facing downward, should be placed over its mouth.
Having smeared the mouths of both with clay, one should then dry them.

children.text: uparisthe tato bhāṇḍe nāḍikāṃ tu niveśayet ||
children.translated_text: Then, in the upper vessel, one should insert a tube.

children.text: ekāṃ tu nāḍikāṃ prājño yatnataḥ kuṇḍalīkṛtām
children.translated_text: The wise man should carefully coil one tube,
place it in a water trough, pierce it, and then insert it.
At the mouth of a glass flask one should properly kindle the fire.
This is to be done until the essence of the substance in the jar becomes vapor here.
Having put an inverted pot above the vessel of the apparatus, one should seal it.
The apparatus called ḍamaruka is useful for making mercury ash.
Having placed one pot above another and sealed it properly,
one should put water in the upper pot and kindle fire below.
This is the vidyādhara apparatus, used for extracting from cinnabar.

children.text: iha rasakarpūrakriyāyāṃ jalam uparisthālyāṃ na deyaṃ rasasya yathārūpasyaiva tatra pātanāt
children.translated_text: Here, in the operation for rasakarpūra, water should not be put in the upper pot, because the mercury there is to be distilled in its very own form.
But in the lower and transverse distillation apparatuses, it will be taught among the mercury-processing operations.
With a circumference of eight aṅgulas and a height of ten aṅgulas,
below the neck there should be a water-holder raised four aṅgulas.
The mouth of that upper vessel
should be inserted into the mouth of the lower vessel, whose back is sixteen aṅgulas broad.
On the sides, with buffalo milk, powder, iron-rust, and molasses,
one should smear and dry the joint, and put water in the water-holder.
This is to be set on the stove; it is called the distillation apparatus.
Then the wise man, after smearing and setting the upper vessel in water,
should carefully produce downward distillation with blazing forest cow-dung cakes.
When mercury falls into a lamp set on a clay platform inside the kacchapa apparatus,
that is called the dīpikā apparatus.
This is used in the place of transverse distillation.
Thus the distillation apparatuses have been described.
Now the apparatuses for distilling the essences and oils of metals, secondary metals, minerals, and secondary minerals are described: siddhasāra, garbhasāra, that born from Paramānandamūrti,
those called pātāla and ākāśa, śrīrañjaka and karuṇākara,

children.text: vāruṇī jyotir ityādi yantrāṇi syur anekadhā
children.translated_text: vāruṇī, jyotis, and many other kinds of apparatuses.
One should set a deep vessel filled with paste on a stove.
By the path of a side tube from it, drops of the melted essence
fall; the apparatus by which this happens is called siddhasāra.
The paste is produced from medicines for stupefaction, killing, and binding.
Likewise, a deep vessel with a perforated lid
is covered by another vessel, with a small jacket in the middle.
For the distillation of vapor-drops, they call this garbhasāra.
This too is precisely for precipitating the essence from a paste.

children.text: tathaiva pārśvanālī tu dīrghā pātrāntaraṃ gatā
children.translated_text: Likewise the side-tube is long and goes into another vessel;
because the falling of liquid occurs from it, that is called the <s>paramānanda</s> form.
Here there is precipitation of essences by means of acidic, alkaline, and kāñjika liquids.
A vessel filled with an oily substance, perforated, is placed in another vessel,
set in a pit, with fire above: this apparatus is called the <s>pātāla</s> apparatus.

children.text: atrāgnir upalānāṃ snigdhadravyaṃ gandhatālādicūrṇaṃ jayapālakampillakādibījacūrṇaṃ vā kṣīrasiktaśuṣkam
children.translated_text: Here the fire is from cow-dung cakes; the oily substance is powder of gandhaka, tāla and the like, or powder of seeds such as jayapāla and kampillaka, soaked in milk and dried.
“Perforated” means that the hole here should be understood as being at the bottom of the vessel.
This is specifically for the precipitation of oil.
With fire above, half of a pot, a potsherd, is placed facing it;
inverted, raised up, tied with cloth, its mouth is covered like a lid or bowl.
The powdered substance placed inside the cloth liquefies and falls downward
into another vessel, of glass or the like: this apparatus is called the <s>ākāśa</s> apparatus.
Or at its mouth there is a glass bottle, perforated below and furnished with cloth.
Here the powder is powder of processed gandhaka and the like, or something else.
Here too the fire is just from cow-dung cakes.
This too is solely for making oil drip down.

children.text: mṛttikādikūpī vālukāyantre sthitā uparilambamānasakalkaghaṭādhaśchidrā dravabinduparipatadrasādidravyā yadi ca syāttadāpyākāśayantram uktam
children.translated_text: If a clay or similar bottle, standing in a sand apparatus, has above it a hanging pot containing paste, perforated below, so that drops of liquid from mercury and other substances fall, then that also is called an <s>ākāśa</s> apparatus.
In a cooking pot filled with coloring liquid one should set
a vessel made of clay or glass, deep, high, and well-shaped.
Having placed there a tripod furnished with fine holes,
one should put gandhaka powder there and burn it at once with a heated sharp rod.

children.text: saṃdahya sadyas tatpātropari pātraṃ ca tadvidham
children.translated_text: Then over that vessel one should place another vessel of the same kind
and cover it so that the container of that vessel sinks into the liquid.
The smoky essence adheres inside its bottom, and one should proceed in that way.
The oil flowing swiftly through the holes also falls into the middle vessel.
This is the <s>śrīrañjaka</s> apparatus, kept secret in all tantras.
The word “gandha” is indicative; tāla, śilā, and the like are also suitable here.
Gandhaka and the other substances should indeed be processed with divine herbs.
The tripod here is made of glass or similar material.
A deep vessel containing paste is set on the stove and concealed;
with the liquids that drip down at its edge into the cooking pot, it becomes the <s>karuṇākara</s> apparatus.
Having set the mouths of two bottles crosswise, with fire kindled beneath one,

children.text: tataḥ kṣāradravo 'nyasyāṃ pated vāruṇikaṃ ca tat ||
children.translated_text: then the alkaline liquid falls into the other; that is the <s>vāruṇika</s> apparatus.
Under a small pot there is lamp-fire, and above there is a bottle placed in a hole;
for precipitating the essence of tāla and the like, this is remembered as the <s>jyotis</s> apparatus.
In a brick-lined pit set on the stove, concealed by another vessel,
the essence of tāla and the like falls down; that is called the <s>sādhya</s> apparatus.

children.text: tālādisattvaṃ cakrasaikatādiyantreṣvapi bhavatītyādyanekadhā buddhyā yantrāṇi jñeyāni
children.translated_text: Since the essence of tāla and the like can also be obtained in cakra, saikata, and other apparatuses, many kinds of apparatus should be understood by intelligent consideration.
It holds four prasthas of water and has a channel four aṅgulas wide;
this is known as the pot-apparatus, and it is remembered as a moistening apparatus.
Now the apparatuses for digesting mercury are described.
Among them, the sand apparatus is described in the <s>Rasendracūḍāmaṇi</s>.
A chamber below with many holes, and a chamber above the pit;
sand placed in a vessel and reaching up to the neck: that is the sand apparatus.
But in the <s>Rasasāra</s> this same apparatus is called the wheel apparatus.
Having filled a potsherd with sand, one should place on top of it

children.text: aparaṃ kharparaṃ tatra śanair mṛdvagninā pacet ||
children.translated_text: another potsherd; there one should cook slowly with gentle fire.

children.text: pacet kṣārais tathā mūtrair lavaṇaṃ ca viḍaṃ tathā
children.translated_text: One should cook with alkalis, with urine, with salt, and with viḍa salt as well;
this apparatus is called <s>haṃsapāka</s> by the best of the vārttikas.
A glass flask seven aṅgulas high, smeared with clay and cloth to a thickness of one aṅgula,
and dried, should be filled to three parts.
It is set in sand inside a vessel a span deep;
one should fill the rest of the vessel and cover it with other materials.
One should close the mouth of the vessel with a small lid, smear the joint with clay, and cook it
on a stove until the grass placed on the back of the lid burns away.
This indeed is the sand apparatus; that apparatus has salt as its support.

children.text: spaṣṭārthastu rasendracintāmaṇau niravadhinipīḍitamṛdambarādipariliptām atikaṭhinakācaghaṭīm agre vakṣyamāṇaprakārāṃ rasagarbhiṇīm adhastarjanyaṅgulipramāṇacchidrāyām anurūpasthālikāyām āropya chidrasya parito dvitryaṅgulimitena lavaṇena nirantarālīkāryākaraṇapuraḥsaraṃ sikatābhirāgalaṃ paripūrya vardhamānakam āropaṇīyaṃ kramataśca tricaturāṇi pañcaṣāṇi vā vāsarāṇi jvalanajvālayā pacanīyam ityekaṃ yantram
children.translated_text: The clearer meaning in the <s>Rasendracintāmaṇi</s> is this: a very hard glass flask containing mercury, thickly coated with clay, cloth, and the like under unremitting pressure, prepared in the manner to be described later, is placed in a fitting cooking pot that has a hole below measuring the breadth of an index finger. Around the hole, after making it continuous with two or three aṅgulas of salt and before forming the opening, it is filled completely up to the neck with sand; a raised cover is to be placed on it, and it should be cooked gradually by a flame for three, four, five, or six days. This is one apparatus.

children.text: kūpī ca tatraiva kācamṛttikayoḥ kūpī hemno 'yastārayorapi iti kvacit ||
children.translated_text: A bottle there may be of glass or clay; in some places it is also said to be a bottle of gold, iron, or copper.
A glass flask containing mercury, with its mouth closed, covered with clay and cloth to a thickness of one aṅgula,
and purified, should be filled to three parts.
It is set in sand inside a vessel a span deep;
one should fill that vessel with three other coverings and wrap it around.
One should close the mouth of the vessel with a small lid, smear the joint with clay, and cook it
on a stove until the grass placed on the back of the jewel-like lid is brought away or burnt off.
This indeed is the sand apparatus; that apparatus has salt as its support.
Having carefully placed it in a vessel filled with five āḍhakas of sand,
<s>rasa</s>-globules and the like are cooked; this is called the sand apparatus.
Likewise, because salt is inserted, it is called the salt apparatus.
Or else, after the mouth of a copper vessel has been coated inside with <s>rasa</s>,
one should smear the joint at the bottom of the vessel with clay and salt alone.
Filling that vessel with sharp salt, or with alkalis, one should cook it as before.
In this way it becomes the salt apparatus, praised for operations on <s>rasa</s>.
A glass bottle, its body smeared with cloth-pounded clay and dried,
and its belly filled with <s>rasa</s> and the like, should be set in place.
It should be placed carefully in a strong pot whose bottom is smeared with clay;

children.text: ā kaṇṭhaṃ kūpikāṃ tatra vālukābhiḥ prapūrayet ||
children.translated_text: there one should fill the bottle up to the neck with sand.
Below the vessel one should kindle the fire according to the proper time and sequence.
This has been described by the wise under the name sand apparatus.

children.text: vṛntākākāramūṣe dve tayoḥ kaṇṭhād adhaḥ khalu
children.translated_text: There are two crucibles shaped like eggplants; below the neck of those two, indeed,
there is a tube about a span long, with its openings sealed with clay.
Into one of them one should put <s>sūta</s> (mercury), and into the other powdered sulfur.
After closing the mouths of the crucibles, one should cook them in the sand apparatus.
One should kindle the fire beneath the sulfur; this is remembered as the balance apparatus.
Having made holes on the four sides of the tube for the smoke to escape,

children.text: vidhāya vartulaṃ gartaṃ mallam atra nidhāya ca
children.translated_text: and having made a circular pit, one should place a shallow earthen pan there.
There one should set a good brick in the middle, furnished with a hollow.
Around the hollow one should make a rim a finger high.

children.text: garbhe sūtaṃ vinikṣipya gartāsye vasanaṃ kṣipet ||
children.translated_text: Putting <s>sūta</s> in the cavity, one should place cloth over the mouth of the hollow.
One should put sulfur there and close the mouth with the shallow pan.
Between the pan and the rim one should seal it properly with clay.

children.text: vanopalaiḥ puṭaṃ deyaṃ kapotākhyaṃ na cādhikam
children.translated_text: A heating with forest cow-dung cakes, called pigeon-sized, should be given, and not more.
This indeed is the brick apparatus; by means of it one should digest sulfur.
Having made an earthen covered capsule four fingers long and three fingers broad,

children.text: mṛnmayaṃ saṃpuṭaṃ kṛtvā chāyāśuṣkaṃ ca kārayet ||
children.translated_text: one should have it dried in the shade.
There should be twenty parts of salt and one part of guggulu.
After grinding all this in water, with that very mixture one should smear the inside of the capsule.

children.text: liptvā tatra mukhaṃ ruddhvā garbhayantramidaṃ bhavet
children.translated_text: Having sealed the mouth there, this becomes the womb apparatus.
This womb apparatus is for the digestion of piṣṭī.
A cup shaped like a ladle, joined with a long handle,
is the ladle apparatus; it accomplishes the purification of sulfur.
This same apparatus, furnished with a bent handle,
is designated the pālikā apparatus by those skilled in <s>rasatantra</s>.
A round iron cup, with an upward rod whose tip is bent,
is indeed this pālikā apparatus, used for digesting bali.
There they say: this also, with the fire of a lamp, makes black <s>rasa</s> ash within the time of one ghaṭikā.

children.text: tatra lohapātre gandhakaṃ drāvayitvā pārado deyaḥ
children.translated_text: There, sulfur should be melted in an iron vessel, and mercury should be added.
Afterwards it should be combined with an iron rod and prepared.
A broad potsherd, properly wide, and in its middle

children.text: ālavālaṃ mṛdā kṛtvā tanmadhye pāradaṃ nyaset ||
children.translated_text: a basin made of clay: in the middle of that one should place mercury.
It is prescribed for the complete digestion of sulfur and the other substances of <s>rasa</s>.
One should obtain a firm, very broad vessel filled with water.

children.text: tadantaḥ kharparaṃ nyasya suvistīrṇaṃ navaṃ dṛḍham ||
children.translated_text: Inside it one should place a new, firm potsherd, very broad.

children.text: viḍaṃ dattvā tadupari kṣipedvā jambhajaṃ rasam
children.translated_text: After putting viḍa on it, one should place over that the <s>rasa</s> born from jambu, or mercury.
One should put viḍa above it, and then an iron bowl,
or one made of lodestone, having the form of a thin plate.
Having placed it above with its face downward, one should smear it properly.

children.text: khaṭīṃ paṭuṃ sudhāṃ bhaktaṃ piṣṭvā samyagvimudrayet
children.translated_text: Grinding chalk, sharp salt, lime, and cooked rice, one should seal it thoroughly.
Above it, the potsherd should be filled with embers produced from forest fuel.
This is the water-tortoise procedure; now it will be explained clearly.
The measure of the lower pot, in length, should be twelve fingers.
It should be sixteen fingers wide, with four pegs at the mouth.
Filling that pot with water, one should bury it in the ground.
Above it one should place the mouth of a bowl upon the pegs.

children.text: adhobhāṇḍe jale magnaṃ śarāvaṃ ca tathā bhavet ||
children.translated_text: Thus the bowl should be immersed in the water in the lower vessel.
This water-tortoise apparatus is commended for the work of digestion.
This very same is the somānala apparatus.
That has been stated by <s>Devendragiri</s>.
A vessel should be properly fashioned to receive gajavellī, broad and facing downward;
an attractive covering like that is here called somānala.
Having placed in the middle of a water-filled vessel a broad potsherd or pot-fragment,

children.text: tadupari viḍamadhyagataḥ sthāpyaḥ sūto mṛdaḥ kuṇḍyām ||
children.translated_text: above it, in the middle of viḍa, <s>sūta</s> should be placed in an earthen basin.
Covering it with a small iron bowl whose joint has been smeared with sharp salt and clay,
one should fill that potsherd or pot-fragment with embers made from khadira and kokila wood.
This apparatus, with water and fire in its interior, is for binding <s>sūta</s>.

children.text: sthūlāsye mṛnmaye pātre ā pākaṃ toyage nyaset ||
children.translated_text: In a wide-mouthed earthen vessel, placed in water, it should remain until it is cooked.
It may be yellow, or endowed with those qualities, and free from sand and the like.
Fire is above, water below, and the collection of <s>rasa</s> is in the middle.
It is called somānala, combined with the paired airy essence.

children.text: tato mākṣikasattvaṃ tu pādāṃśaṃ tatra jārayet
children.translated_text: Then one should digest in it a quarter-part of the essence of mākṣika.
Burnt conch, treated with the milks of arka and exposed a hundred times to the sun,

children.text: tataḥ pañcapuṭaiḥ pakvaṃ ruddhvā ruddhvātha sampuṭe ||
children.translated_text: Then, cooked through five puṭas, repeatedly sealed up in a closed crucible...
Having added an equal amount of ṭaṅkaṇa, one should treat it with the group of sour substances.

children.text: rājāvartaṃ pravālaṃ ca daradaṃ gandhakaṃ śilā ||
children.translated_text: Rājāvarta, coral, darada, sulphur, and śilā:

children.text: pañcānāṃ tu samaṃ cūrṇaṃ śaṃkhatulyaṃ niyojayet
children.translated_text: one should apply a powder of the five in equal parts, equal to the conch-shell substance.
All of that should be ground with the sour group for three days.

children.text: ayaṃ mahāviḍaḥ khyātaḥ khoṭānāṃ jāraṇe hitaḥ
children.translated_text: This is known as mahāviḍa, useful for the digestion of khoṭas.
Having made an iron vessel eight aṅgulas across and eight aṅgulas high,

children.text: kaṇṭhādho dvyaṃgule deśe galādhāre hi tatra ca ||
children.translated_text: at a place two aṅgulas below the neck, there at the support of the throat,
one should insert thin iron rods crosswise, running transversely.
On top of them one should place thin leaves of gold.
Below the leaves one should put the fumigant that will be described right here.
One should cover that vessel with another vessel turned upside down.

children.text: mṛdā vilipya sandhiṃ ca vahniṃ prajvālayedadhaḥ
children.translated_text: Having smeared the joint with clay, one should kindle fire below.
By that, all the leaves are killed according to the stated method.

children.text: rasaścarati vegena drutaṃ garbhe dravanti ca
children.translated_text: The rasa moves swiftly, and, liquefied, they melt in the womb.
The fumigation of gold leaves is first taught with the soot of gandhaka, alaka, and śilā, or with dead snakes.
The fumigation of gold leaves has been proclaimed first.
For silver, one should fumigate silver leaves with dead tin.
And one should fumigate with other secondary minerals as appropriate.
This fumigation apparatus is taught for the accomplishment of rasa through digestion.

children.text: sthūlasthālyāṃ jalaṃ kṣiptvā vāso baddhvā mukhe dṛḍham
children.translated_text: Having put water in a large earthen pot and tied cloth firmly over its mouth,

children.text: tatra svedyaṃ vinikṣipya tanmukhaṃ prapidhāya ca ||
children.translated_text: one should place there the substance to be steamed and cover its mouth.
One should kindle fire underneath; that apparatus is called kanduka.
Other wise men call this a steaming apparatus.

children.text: yadvā sthālyāṃ jalaṃ kṣiptvā tṛṇaṃ dattvā mukhopari
children.translated_text: Or, having put water in an earthen pot and placed straw over the mouth,
one should put in the substance to be steamed and cover it with a lid.
One should kindle fire underneath; that apparatus is remembered as kanduka.

children.text: sthūlasthālyāṃ dravaṃ kṣiptvā vāso baddhvā mukhe dṛḍham
children.translated_text: Having put liquid in a large earthen pot and tied cloth firmly over the mouth,

children.text: tatra svedyaṃ vinikṣipya pidhānyā prapidhāya ca ||
children.translated_text: one should put the substance to be steamed there and cover it with a lid.
One should kindle fire below there; that is the kanduka apparatus.
Other wise men call this a steaming apparatus.
In a long vessel with a bent tube, one should place the king of rasa.
One should carefully connect that tube into the interior of another pot.
Then one should carefully seal the mouth of the small vessel containing the rasa.
Then one should kindle a strong fire beneath the vessel of rasa.
And one should fill the other vessel with clear, cool waters.
This apparatus is declared to be called oblique distillation.
One should put rasa in a vessel fitted with a long tube bent downward.
That tube should indeed be inserted inside the belly of another vessel.
Then, having properly sealed the mouths of the two vessels there with clay,
one should kindle an intense fire below the rasa-pot.
Into the other vessel one should pour sweet, cool water.
This is called oblique distillation by the practitioners.
For distillation there is a downward vessel with a twelve-aṅgula mouth, very round, truly firm, expanded in its belly,
and provided with a lip two aṅgulas in measure.
Furnished at the bottom with all the stated groups, provided with holes and a firm circular stand,

children.text: ūrdhvagā ca jaṭharojjvālā ghaṭī tūrdhvapātanavidhau praśasyate ||
children.translated_text: and rising upward, with flame in its belly, the vessel is praised in the procedure of upward distillation.
Having put rasa in the lower vessel, one should join the mouths of these two.
After wrapping the joint and drying it, one should then set it on the stove.
Having placed a small tube in the hole of the circular stand, one should smear the joint.
Into the middle of the stand one should pour water through the opening of the small tube.
One should draw out the heated water and put in cold water.
This upward-distillation apparatus has been described by those who know rasa.
Fine old iron-rust powder, made like an ointment and treated with a decoction of babbūla,
and mixed with powdered jaggery,

children.text: iyaṃ hi jalamṛtproktā durbhedyā salilaiḥ khalu ||
children.translated_text: is called water-clay; it is truly hard for waters to pierce.
Eight aṅgulas in circumference and ten aṅgulas in breadth,
with a water-reservoir four aṅgulas high below the neck,
the lower vessel's mouth of the vessel placed above
should be inserted into the sixteen-aṅgula-wide opening on the back.
On the sides, with buffalo-milk powder, iron-rust powder, and molasses,

children.text: liptvā viśoṣayet sandhiṃ jalādhāre jalaṃ kṣipet
children.translated_text: having smeared and dried the joint, one should put water in the water-reservoir.
One should set this on the stove; it is called a distillation apparatus.
The apparatus known as Vidyādhara is to be understood as made from the enclosure of two earthen pots.
Having made a four-mouthed stove, one should place the apparatus-vessel in it.
Having put the medicine there, one should close the mouth of the vessel.
The apparatus named Vidyādhara is so proclaimed by those who know the tantra.
Having put rasa in the lower earthen pot, one should place over its mouth
an earthen pot facing upward, properly sealed with soft clay.

children.text: ūrdhvaṃ sthālyāṃ jalaṃ kṣiptvā cullyāmāropya yatnataḥ
children.translated_text: Having put water in the upper pot and carefully set it on the stove,
one should kindle fire underneath for as long as five praharas.
Then, when it has cooled by itself, one should take the excellent rasa from the apparatus.
This apparatus called Vidyādhara is described by those who know it.
Having placed the <s>rasa</s> in a potsherd set in the middle of a vessel filled with water,

children.text: balimadhyagataṃ kumudīnihitaṃ caṣakeṇa bhṛśaṃ pidadhīta tataḥ ||
children.translated_text: situated in the midst of bali and placed in a water-lily-like arrangement, one should then cover it firmly with a cup.
After the joints have been smeared with water and clay, one should kindle a fire with khadira and kokila wood,

children.text: paridīpya bhṛśaṃ supaced gaditaṃ kila kacchapasaṃjñakayantram idam ||
children.translated_text: and cook it thoroughly. This, it is said, is the apparatus called kacchapa.
The apparatus called kacchapa is for accomplishing the digestion of bali;
it has been described by the teachers of <s>rasa</s> as bestowing success in <s>rasa</s>.
One skilled in the proper technique should fashion a vessel shaped like a mṛdaṅga drum, hollow inside and very firm,
by the proper method.
It should be joined on one side with a turning device,
and on the two sides there should be two side-rings capable of revolving.

children.text: kārayecca tato yuktyā sūtaṃ gandhaṃ ca nikṣipet
children.translated_text: Then one should make it properly, and place <s>sūta</s> and sulfur in it;
one should fit the turning lid very firmly in place.

children.text: tato narotsedhamitau stambhau bhūmau tu vinyaset
children.translated_text: Then a learned physician who knows the procedure should set two pillars in the ground,
each as high as a man, facing one another there.
Then he should suspend the apparatus from the two pillars, supported by a rod;
this is called the mṛdaṅga apparatus by those who know <s>rasa</s>.
For producing artificial mleccha, those skilled in <s>rasatantra</s>
now especially employ the mṛdaṅga apparatus.
Having smeared <s>sūta</s> inside the upper vessel, and placed water in the lower vessel,

children.text: nikṣipya bhūmau gate ca vidhāya vinyased dṛḍham ||
children.translated_text: one should set it firmly, arranged in a pit in the ground.
There one should strongly kindle the fire with blazing cow-dung cakes;
this is called the downward-sublimation apparatus by those who know <s>rasa</s>.
Then, when it has been smeared and placed in water in the upper vessel, the wise man
should carefully bring about the downward fall with blazing forest cow-dung cakes.
Above the lower pot one should place another bowl facing downward,
a small bowl whose flattened bottom inside has been smeared with mercury.

children.text: kṣiptvā taṃ paṃkile garte jvālayenmūrdhni pāvakam
children.translated_text: After putting it in a muddy pit, one should light a fire on its top;
this indeed is called the downward-sublimation apparatus.
One should place a vessel inside a vessel whose interior is filled with water,
with small openings on the sides and filled with a decoction of the substance.
Then, placing it on a stove, one should kindle a fire below;
thereafter one should dry up the decoction until it reaches the state of powder.
Because steaming is done with vapor by those skilled in <s>rasatantra</s>,
therefore this apparatus is known by the name bāṣpasvedana, steam-sudation.
This apparatus is described as a means for producing the essence of particular forest herbs,
for the convenience of physicians.
It is sixteen fingers wide, equal in length to a hasta;
it is remembered as the koṣṭhī apparatus, used for the precipitation of metallic essences.
In the furnace, fully packed with firm charcoal and with a draft from below,
one should kindle the fire in due measure through the flame-channel.

children.text: gāraṃ dagdhaṃ tuṣā dagdhā dagdhā valmīkamṛttikā
children.translated_text: Burnt brick-dust, burnt husk, burnt termite-mound clay,

children.text: viḍam aṅgārakaḥ kiṭṭaṃ vajreṇāpi na bhidyate ||
children.translated_text: viḍa, charcoal, and slag cannot be split even by a diamond.
Brick-dust is clay that has long disintegrated in water.
Six parts of burnt charcoal and one part of black clay,
together with viḍa, charcoal, and slag, are called a diamond crucible.

children.text: tuṣaṃ vastraṃ samaṃ dagdhaṃ mṛttikā caturaṃśikā
children.translated_text: Equal parts of burnt husk and cloth, with clay as a fourth part,
joined with kūrma stone, are called a diamond crucible.
There should be one part of iron slag and two parts of burnt husk;
with three parts of clay added, a little kupya is supplied.

children.text: ekatra kuṭṭayet sarvaṃ mṛttikā vajravad bhavet
children.translated_text: One should pound everything together in one place; the clay becomes like diamond.

children.text: tayā mūṣā prakartavyā trividhā sādhakena tu ||
children.translated_text: With it the practitioner should make a crucible of three kinds.
Iron slag, burnt husk, shell-powder, and sugar,
these are in equal parts, with clay in an equal quantity.
A crucible bond should be made; by blowing it attains diamond-like hardness.
One part powdered brick, and clay in an equal part:
a crucible bond should be made; by blowing it attains diamond-like hardness.
Three parts clay, two parts salt, and one part thoroughly burnt husk and stone,
with half a part of slag, should be well pounded; one should make a diamond crucible for precipitating essence.
A round, cow's-udder-shaped form is called a diamond crucible.
One part termite-mound clay, two parts husk-ash,
one part iron slag, and one part white stone,
together with human hair, should be ground with goat's milk.

children.text: yāmadvayaṃ dṛḍhaṃ mardyaṃ tena mūṣātha saṃpuṭam ||
children.translated_text: It should be firmly rubbed for two yāmas; from it one should make a crucible and then a covered capsule.
After drying it, putting in <s>rasa</s>, and sealing the joint with those pastes,
it is well known as a diamond crucible for the proper calcination of <s>sūta</s>.
Husk and the rest should be burnt until they become black.

children.text: tuṣaṃ vastraṃ samaṃ dagdhaṃ tatpādāṃśena mṛttikām ||
children.translated_text: Equal amounts of husk and cloth should be burnt, and clay should be one quarter of that.
Stone should be one quarter of that; with the liquids of vajravallī, for a day
one should grind it and prepare a crucible called vajra for binding <s>rasa</s>.

children.text: gaurī dagdhā tuṣā dagdhā dagdhā valmīkamṛttikā
children.translated_text: Burnt gaurī, burnt husk, burnt termite-mound clay,

children.text: gajāśvānāṃ malaṃ dagdhaṃ yāvad ākṛṣṇatāṃ gatam ||
children.translated_text: and the dung of elephants and horses should be burnt until they become black.
Leaves of pāṣāṇabheda and black clay should be in equal measure.

children.text: vajravallīdravair mardyaṃ niśāṃ saṃśoṣya ca dṛḍham ||
children.translated_text: It should be ground with the juices of vajravallī through the night and dried until firm.

children.text: tena koṣṭhīṃ vakranālīṃ vajramūṣāṃ ca kārayet
children.translated_text: With that one should make a furnace, a bent tube, and a diamond crucible.
A glass bottle or an iron bottle should be four, five, or nine fingers in measure,
smeared seven times and dried; it should be smeared with that same clay and rag mixture.
Ant-hill earth, charcoal filling, iron slag,
and white stone: all that should be powdered in equal quantity.
One should add burnt husk equal to all of it and grind it thoroughly with water.
One should make a sealing capsule for crucibles and the like, and a coating for all the joints.
That which has the form of a potter's vessel, is firm, and is thoroughly baked,

children.text: pakvamūṣeti sā proktā sā sarvatra vipācane ||
children.translated_text: is called a baked <s>mūṣā</s> (crucible); it is used everywhere for cooking operations.

children.text: prakāśā cāndhamūṣā tu prākṛtā dvividhā smṛtā
children.translated_text: A <s>mūṣā</s> is remembered as of two ordinary kinds: open and closed.
The open <s>mūṣā</s>, O goddess, has the shape of a shallow bowl,
and it is praised in medicine for drawing off or removing substances.
The closed one should be made like the shape of a cow's teat,
provided with a lid and with its top somewhat raised.
For smearing leaves, for portions, and likewise for combining paired substances,
that same vessel, furnished with holes, slow and deep, is suitable for <s>sāraṇa</s> (transference or extraction).
A long <s>mūṣā</s> should be made for <s>sāraṇa</s> and for the falling of <s>sattva</s> (metallic essence).
One should make the capsule compact; potsherds are useful for burning.
A <s>mūṣā</s> of good iron should be made to the measure of a half-cubit.

children.text: mūṣordhvaṃ saṃpuṭaṃ kṛtvā saṃdhilepaṃ tu kārayet ||
children.translated_text: Having made a capsule above the <s>mūṣā</s>, one should apply a sealing coat to the joint.
In a perforated capsule, a tube should be like the flower of <s>unmatta</s>.
There should be two parts of sesame ash, together with an equal part of brick.
This is to be known as the ash-crucible, useful for purifying <s>tāra</s> (silver).
A <s>mūṣā</s> six fingers in measure is called <s>mañjūṣā</s>.
The crucible shaped like a box is low in form and broad.
Having buried that <s>mūṣā</s> in the ground, one should then give a <s>puṭa</s> (heating) above it.
Straight, spherical, and containing the substance for <s>puṭa</s>-heating in its interior,
it is called the spherical crucible, quickly producing a fluid form.

children.text: dagdhā tuṣā lohakiṭṭaṃ gairikaṃ ca kulālamṛt
children.translated_text: Burnt husks, iron slag, red ochre, and potter's clay,
white clay and chalk in equal quantity: when dried in shade, this is a crucible-clay.
Ant-hill earth, soot, red ochre, chalk, and sharp salt:
these five clays are taught for <s>rasa</s>-work.
Earth from a serpent mound, clay, and rough iron slag,
together with husks produced from rice grain and carefully burnt.

children.text: kṛṣṇā raktā ca pītā ca śuklavarṇā ca mṛttikā
children.translated_text: Clay may be black, red, yellow, or white in color.

children.text: ādyā śreṣṭhā kaniṣṭhāntyā madhyamā madhyamā matā ||
children.translated_text: The first is best, the last is inferior, and the middle two are regarded as middling.
Clay mixed with burnt grain husks is indeed suitable for a furnace,
or one made with a bent tube is recommended, O beautiful goddess.

children.text: gārā dagdhā tuṣā dagdhā dagdhā valmīkamṛttikā
children.translated_text: Burnt mortar, burnt husks, burnt ant-hill earth,

children.text: ajāśvānāṃ malaṃ dagdhaṃ dagdhā mṛtkṛṣṇatāṃ gatā ||
children.translated_text: the burnt dung of goats and horses, and burnt clay that has become black:

children.text: vāsakasya ca patrāṇi valmīkasya mṛdā saha
children.translated_text: the leaves of <s>vāsaka</s>, together with ant-hill earth,
should be ground with diamond-water until it becomes smooth.
One should knead it with that and fasten together a bent tube and a small furnace.
A clay that is smooth, sticky, heavy, black, and conquers everything is best.
Or it may be yellow, endowed with those qualities, and free from sand and the like.

children.text: yā mṛttikā dagdhatuṣopalena śikhitrakairvā hayaladdinā ca
children.translated_text: The clay which, with burnt husk, stones, sparks, or horse-dung,

children.text: lauhena daṇḍena ca kuṭṭitā sā sādhāraṇā syāt khalu mūṣikārtham
children.translated_text: is beaten with an iron rod: that indeed is suitable in general for making a crucible.
Here the clay may be potter's clay or ant-hill earth,
with chalk, sharp salt, and slag, kneaded with buffalo milk.
In fire, the clay truly becomes able to withstand the fierce heat of fire,
when kneaded thoroughly with a decoction of <s>babbūla</s> made like a paste.
Fine powder of old slag, combined with powdered jaggery:
this is called water-clay, and it is hard to break even by water.
Another clay is prepared with clay, cotton, and slag,
with lac, powdered clay, salt, jaggery, black gram, water, and the like.
One should knead it with old cotton grass and sheep's milk.
Another clay is kneaded also with the juice of a hen's egg.
These two clays are excellent for coating a glass bottle.
Powder of green vitriol, iron rust, borax, and sal ammoniac,
and the five salts: one should grind the clay with lemon juices.
When like foam, it is called the clay for coating a <s>ḍamaru</s>-apparatus.
Black clay from a potter's hand, yellow clay, and <s>karambhaka</s>,
human hair, <s>kāgara</s>, and husks: one should grind these.
With sour ferment made from grapes, jaggery, and the like, it is called diamond-crucible clay.
Chalk, salt, red ochre, alum, and powdered brick:
these five clays are taught as the cause of the perfection of gold.
When smeared and <s>puṭa</s>-heated with them, the gold becomes divine.
Two parts of <s>mokṣakṣāra</s>, together with a part of brick,
and parts of clay are excellent for the purification of <s>tāra</s>, O fair one.
Mixed with the red group, soaked in the red group,
and coated with a paste made from the red group, it is excellent for all purifications.
Mixed with the white group, soaked in the white group,
and coated with a paste made from the white group, it is excellent for white purifications.
For digestion, they desire clay mixed with the <s>viḍa</s> group.
One should perform extraction with a coating of the red group.
One should make a crucible coating with poison, borax, and guñjā seeds.
In an open crucible, or else, one should apply a charcoal coating.
Having placed the substance in that crucible, the wise person should melt it down.
The coating for a color-<s>puṭa</s>, O goddess, is made with red clay, rock salt, earth, and <s>bhūkhaga</s>.
Breast milk, borax, sauvīra, lāṅgalī, and girikarṇikā...
Citraka, karavīra, sārivā, kṣīriṇī, and poison:
with these, when a crucible is smeared, there is a great medicine for the purpose of binding.
Chalk, salt, flour of māṣa beans, and also old jaggery,
linseed and powdered stone are praised in clay coatings and the like.

children.text: saṃdhiṃ vilepayed yatnānmṛdā vastreṇa caiva hi ||
children.translated_text: One should carefully smear the joint with clay and also with cloth.
At the joint of the crucible and its lid one should put glass and ṭaṅkaṇa.
Then one should apply fire above; the adhesion of the joint becomes very strong.

children.text: rasapaddhatiṭīkākārastvāha vālukāyantrakūpaṃ tu mṛttikayā dṛḍhāgnisahaṃ kāryam
children.translated_text: But the commentator on the <s>Rasapaddhati</s> says: the pit of the sand apparatus should be made of clay that can withstand a strong fire.
And it has been said:
White stones, husk, chāyā, variegated pieces, and hemp cloths,
laddī, slag, and black clay should be combined in the clay for the bottle.
White stones means white stones.
Chāyā means black clay; alternatively potter's clay should be taken.

children.text: tuṣamekabhāgaṃ śvetamṛttikaikabhāgā kṛṣṇamṛttikaikabhāgā vastrakhaṇḍam ekabhāgaṃ kuṭṭayitvā lepaḥ kāryaḥ
children.translated_text: Having pounded one part husk, one part white clay, one part black clay, and one part pieces of cloth, a coating should be made.
But pieces of cloth should be applied just seven times.

children.text: evaṃ vālukāyantrasyāpi mṛtkarpaṭāni madhye chidraṃ ca kāryam
children.translated_text: In this way clay-and-cloth wrappings should also be made for the sand apparatus, with a hole in the middle.
Sand measuring five āḍhakas should be put in.
The measure is the same also in the salt apparatus.
Concerning bottles, in the <s>Rasendracintāmaṇi</s>:
A coating made of kīlāla and iron, with chalk and salt in excess,
and <s>Śaivālabhakṣya</s> too says:
Two parts of husk should be taken, and one part of pieces of cloth;

children.text: mṛdaṃ ca triguṇīkṛtya jalaṃ dattvā vimardayet ||
children.translated_text: making clay three times as much, one should add water and rub it together.

children.text: narakeśaṃ samaṃ kṛtvā kiṃcit tāvat prakuṭṭayet
children.translated_text: Having made human hair equal in amount, one should pound it a little,
until the lump of clay becomes similar in appearance to wax.

children.text: yathā na śuṣkatāmeti tathā yatnaṃ samācaret
children.translated_text: One should take care so that it does not become dry.

children.text: evaṃ saptadinād ūrdhvaṃ mṛdaṃ yoge prayojayet ||
children.translated_text: Thus after seven days one should employ the clay in the mixture.
For smearing bottles and the like, and also apparatuses, the physician should proceed in order.
Make water and the exudation of babbūla equal to the flour.
Make pure iron slag, resembling collyrium, equal to those two.

children.text: mudrāṃ vai vāriyantrasya siddhyarthaṃ durlabhāṃ kuru ||
children.translated_text: Prepare a seal of the water apparatus, hard to obtain, for success.
Here it is never split by the combination of water and fire.
And <s>sūtaka</s> does not escape, even with the speed of the fire of dissolution.

children.text: ratnapuṣpābhavaṃ tailaṃ kuḍave dve jalena vai
children.translated_text: Oil produced from ratnapuṣpā, two kuḍavas, together with water,

children.text: prasthena miśritaṃ vahnau tailaśeṣaṃ ca kārayet ||
children.translated_text: mixed with a prastha, should be cooked on the fire until only oil remains.
Into that one should put birch-bark, pounded and resembling collyrium,
one pala, free from dust, bristles, and the like.
And one pala of iron slag, with the lustre of pure collyrium,
should be rubbed with lemon juice; or, for that purpose, one should smear it with that.
And again in that same place:
There should be one part glass, twice as much dead bhāskara,
five parts from rasaka, and six parts washed clay.
Having ground it with the juices of āṭarūṣa, one should make a covered capsule with it.
One should construct a crucible; truly it becomes a fetter for <s>rasa</s>.
It does not go from the midst of the fire, and, with its wings cut, it remains.
A glass bottle is the second; the third is an iron covered capsule.
Ash of palāśa, apāmārga alkali, barley alkali, and sour gruel,

children.text: sauvarcalaṃ ca kāsīsaṃ sāmudraṃ saindhavaṃ tathā ||
children.translated_text: sauvarcala salt, kāsīsa, sea salt, and rock salt,
āsurī, ṭaṅkaṇa, and also navasāra,
camphor and mākṣīka should be made equal in parts.
With the milks of snuhī and arka, O goddess, one should make the crucible coating.
Thus the coating for the digestion of sulfur.
Milk produced from snuhī and arka, brahma seeds, and guggulu;
having added twice as much rock salt, the wise man should rub it together.
Having made an enclosure for the piṣṭaka with this paste, O beautiful one,
and having made a very firm new crucible, of the measure of a bilva fruit,

children.text: ūrdhvādho lavaṇaṃ dattvā mūṣāmadhye rasaṃ kṣipet ||
children.translated_text: he should put salt above and below, and place <s>rasa</s> in the middle of the crucible.
A crucible coating should be applied from powders such as burnt conch.
Having firmly bound the joint of the crucible together with salt-clay,
one should make a coating of lime and have it dried in the shade.
This nigaḍa-binding has been taught; it is not to be told even to one's son.

children.text: atra snuhyarkaprabhavaṃ kṣīraṃ ityatra śigrusarjabhavaṃ kṣāraṃ ityapi pāṭhaḥ
children.translated_text: Here, where the reading is 'milk produced from snuhī and arka,' there is also the reading 'alkali produced from śigru and sarja.'
Brahma means palāśa.
Oil, arka milk, kāhārī, and lāṅgalī are an excellent nigaḍa.
Crow dung, brahma seeds, and lāṅgalī are an excellent nigaḍa.
Bākucī, brahma seeds, the milks of snuhī and arka, and rock salt,
jvālinī and crow dung are another praised nigaḍa.
Salt, ṭaṅkaṇa, alkali, śilā, tālaka, and sulfur,
and likewise amlavetasa, tāpya, and hiṅgula, in equal parts:
joined with the milks of snuhī and arka, one should grind them into the best nigaḍa.
One should wrap the piṣṭikā with one of these nigaḍas.
Placed in an iron crucible, as before, having made a lump, one should pierce it.
'As before' means what is going to be stated.
Lodestone and iron powder, combined with boar's blood:
all that should be put there, and it should be struck with heavy blows.
From the beginning of twilight until sunrise, when the disk of the sun is seen,
it is known as the haṭhamudrā, honored by all perfected beings.
Kroḍa means boar.
Three ṭaṅkas of lodestone should be given, and nine ṭaṅkas of iron rust,
combined with human blood, mixing it again and again.

children.text: ghanena kuṭitaṃ sarvaṃ caturyāmaṃ ca marditam
children.translated_text: Everything is pounded with the solid pestle and rubbed for four yāmas;
it is famous as the haṭhamudrā, the forceful seal, honored by all adepts.
Having obtained iron slag, one should powder six palas of it,
strain it through cloth, and place it in the mortar.
One should add meat together with the bones of goat and sheep,
and pound it with a firm hand, putting the powder in the middle.
When it is like wax, then the seal has become perfected.
Now other seals are described, accomplished by the proper method.
Glass, borax, iron rust, and brick are thoroughly prepared;
with the milks of banyan, arka, and udumbara, in one day it becomes a haṭhā seal.

children.text: audumbarākhyavaṭadugdhapalaṃ palaṃ ca lākṣāpalamṛṣipalaṃ tvatha cumbakasya
children.translated_text: One pala of udumbara and banyan milk, one pala of lac, one pala of ṛṣi, and then one pala of lodestone,
pounded together and mixed with linseed oil, form the seal called madanā for the procedure of digesting <s>sūta</s>.
In four iron vessels, successively, with heated water,
by pouring it from one into the next, one should boil it thoroughly in a pan.
As long as wax settled at the bottom remains, so long it should be kept filled with water.
That wax is declared excellent for coating in water-apparatus and the like.
A wise man should make two pieces of worn, fine cloth,
in a square glass bottle, according to a measure of one and a half and a half.
In the middle, from a quarter part of the baked portion, he should make it broad in two parts,
and set it in the glass bottle, immersed in a mud paste.
When it has been smeared to the thickness of a barley grain, again with firm clay,
one piece of cloth, furnished with a hole in the middle,
should be inserted from the neck of the bottle, and he should level it all around with clay.
Another piece below, in the same way, should be set in the glass bottle.
After drying it in the sun, he should smear it again in the same way with clay.
Again he should apply two cloth-pieces in that same manner.
Having thus dried and fitted three layers of clay and cloth,
he should put in the paste of <s>rasa</s> and the other substances, and carefully make the seal.
Having covered the bottle with ash, leaving aside the opening of the neck-tube,
he should place five or six strongly ignited coals at the neck.
With iron or bamboo tubes he should blow with air from the mouth,
until the glass at the neck of the glass bottle has melted.
With tongs he should level it, carefully closing the joint.
He should make the seal of melted glass, the one devised by <s>Gorakṣa</s>.
Little by little he should remove the coals with tongs.
Then, when the ash has cooled, he should take up the bottle.
It should be fitted as before with four layers of clay and cloth,
smeared with clay mixed with hair and husk, without any hole, and dried.
Having placed it in an apparatus such as the cakra-yantra, he should perform digestion and the other operations.
Thus, through smokeless heating, success is superior by ten million times.
I shall explain the rule for the koṣṭhī stove-apparatus; listen, beloved.
It should have a height of eighteen aṅgulas and an enclosing circumference in due measure,
round like the shape of an anthill and larger at the lower part,
hollow inside like a furnace and furnished with five projecting lugs.
As lugs are made on the top of a rampart, so he should make the lugs.
At the base he should make an outer door.
It should be twelve aṅgulas wide, square on all sides.

children.text: sadvārā culhikā koṣṭhī rasajñeṣu iyaṃ matā ||
children.translated_text: Among knowers of <s>rasa</s>, this stove with a door is considered the koṣṭhī.
A one-mouthed stove is suited to operations such as sublimation.

children.text: culhī tu dvimukhī proktā svedanādiṣu karmasu ||
children.translated_text: A two-mouthed stove is prescribed for operations such as steaming.

children.text: mahāsvedādiṣu tathā culhī tu trimukhī smṛtā
children.translated_text: Likewise, for great steaming and the like, a three-mouthed stove is remembered.
A four-mouthed one is taught for digestion and for the precipitation of metallic essence.
So too the stove called <s>Śrīnātha</s>, with many mouths, is used in digestion.
Sixteen aṅgulas wide and one hasta long, auspicious,
is the furnace for the precipitation of metallic essence, fair one.
There are the ground-holed, many-holed, three-tubed, and eight-tubed kinds,
and, with sixteen bent tubes, it is used in operations on iron and the other metals.
The mouth of the furnace that is large and made a span across,
like the neck of a crane, is called a bent tube.
The bent tube should be at the end of an arm, and at its tip a span in measure.
A suitable bellows should be made as the blower for the sake of metals.
A bamboo tube or iron tube, one hasta long, is auspicious
as the blower for gold and other seeds, with currents of mouth-breath.
But the tube should not be inferior; if made of clay, it should have a long stalk.
With bamboo, khadira, madhūka, and badarī wood,
one should fill the furnace completely with firm charcoal and blow it with wind.
With the bellows, through the flame-channel, he should kindle the fire.
When gold is being smelted, the flame is yellow; in silver, it has a white brilliance.
In copper it is blue-like; in sharp iron it is black in color, queen of gods.
In tin the flame resembles a dove; in lead it has dull smoke.

children.text: śaile tu dhūsarā devi āyase kapilaprabhā ||
children.translated_text: In stone it is gray, goddess; in iron ore it has tawny brilliance.
In lodestone it is smoke-colored; in copper pyrites it is red.
In diamond the flame is of many kinds; in kha-sattva it has a pale brilliance.

children.text: na visphuliṅgā na ca budbudaśca yadā na lekhā paṭalaṃ na śabdāḥ
children.translated_text: When there are no sparks, no bubbles, no streak, no film, and no sounds,

children.text: mūṣāgataṃ ratnasamaṃ sthitaṃ ca tadā viśuddhaṃ pravadanti loham ||
children.translated_text: and when what is in the crucible remains like a jewel, then they declare the metal purified.
The counter-addition should be applied first, and the quenching immediately afterward.

children.text: chādanaṃ tu pratīvāpo niṣekaṃ majjanaṃ viduḥ ||
children.translated_text: Covering is called pratīvāpa; sprinkling is understood as niṣeka and immersion as majjana.

children.text: abhiṣekaṃ tadicchanti snapanaṃ kriyate tu yat
children.translated_text: They call it abhiṣeka, while what is performed as bathing is snapana.

children.text: vāpo niṣekaḥ snapanaṃ drute nirmalatāṃ gate ||
children.translated_text: Vāpa, niṣeka, and snapana are applied when the molten substance has reached purity.

children.text: uṣṇenaiva hi vāñchanti śītalaṃ ca na vāñchati
children.translated_text: They desire it only with heat; they do not desire it cold.
When <s>Vaiśvānara</s>, the fire, becomes white in brilliance and accompanied by sound,

children.text: lohāvartaḥ sa vijñeyaḥ sattvaṃ patati nirmalam
children.translated_text: that should be known as the swirling of metal; the pure metallic essence falls down.
One should blow it with firm charcoal until the metallic essence falls below.

children.text: kadācinna dravetsattvaṃ baddhā piṇḍīṃ dhamet punaḥ
children.translated_text: If sometimes the essence does not melt, one should bind the lump and blow it again.
Thus the rule for fire.
Coals left by fire are remembered as śikhitrā, pāvakocchiṣṭa, and kokila.

children.text: atraviśeṣaḥ jalena siktāścettarhi kokilāḥ anyathā tu pāvakocchiṣṭāḥ
children.translated_text: Here there is a distinction: if they have been sprinkled with water, then they are kokila; otherwise they are pāvakocchiṣṭa.

children.text: te ca vaṃśakhādiramādhūkabadarīdārusaṃbhavaiḥ iti rasārṇavoktā eva
children.translated_text: And these are just those stated in the <s>Rasārṇava</s>, produced from bamboo, khadira, madhūka, and badarī wood.
The plural is meant to indicate the first and so forth; therefore those produced from āmalakī and the like should also be understood.
Thus, coals.
Piṣṭaka, chagaṇa, śāṇa, upala, and likewise utpala,
giriṇḍa, upalaśāṭhi: these are names for well-dried cow dung.
These names refer only to forest cow-dung cakes; otherwise there are names such as gomayopala.
In rasāyana, a puṭa should be given beginning with one hundred and extending to one thousand.
In an operation for destroying disease, it should begin with ten and extend to one hundred.

children.text: śatādipuṭapakṣe mudganibhān dhātukhaṇḍān kṛtvā puṭayet vastrapūtaṃ ca na kuryāt
children.translated_text: When the rule is for puṭas beginning with one hundred, one should make pieces of metal the size of mudga beans and fire them; one should not pass them through cloth.

children.text: puṭaṃ tu bhāvanāṃ vinā nāstīti bhāvanāmātrocyate
children.translated_text: But there is no puṭa without bhāvanā; therefore only bhāvanā is being stated.
With the juices of herbs, until the <s>rasa</s> becomes like mud,
complete saturation is proclaimed as the highest measure of bhāvanā.
But the commentator on the <s>Rasapaddhati</s> says:

children.text: atra sūryapuṭāni prātaḥkālād ārabhya sandhyāparyantaṃ śuṣkamardanena saṃpādanīyāni
children.translated_text: Here, solar puṭas are to be accomplished by dry grinding, beginning in the morning and continuing until evening.

children.text: bhāvanā tu sandhyāyāṃ yathārdratā sampadyate tathā kāryā
children.translated_text: Bhāvanā, however, should be done in the evening so that moistness is produced.

children.text: lohakarmaṇi bhāvanāyāṃ niyamo nāsti mardanasyaiva bhasmasaṃpādakatvāt
children.translated_text: In operations on iron there is no rule for bhāvanā, since grinding alone accomplishes the ash.
In metals, burning with cow-dung cakes as fuel is puṭa.
Saturation with liquid is bhāvanā.
Thus, puṭa and bhāvanā.
A puṭa is the indication of the measure for cooking substances such as <s>rasa</s>.
Cooking that is deficient or excessive is not desired; well-cooked medicine is beneficial.
The non-reversion of iron and the like, increase of qualities, and also sharp potency,
not sinking in water, filling the lines of the fingers: these arise from puṭa.
From puṭa there comes lightness from heaviness, rapid pervasion, and kindling power.
Even more than digested lord mercury, metals have superior quality.
A puṭa with sixteen śikā leaves above, or with husks or cow-dung cakes,
where that is used in the processing of a soft substance, is called lāvakapuṭa.
The puṭa on the surface of the ground that is two spans high,
and just as broad at the bottom, is the kukkuṭaka puṭa.
The puṭa that is given on the ground with eight cow-dung cakes
for the ash of fixed mercury is called kapotapuṭa.
Where a puṭa is given with cow-dung cakes or with husks,
that is called govarapuṭa, for the accomplishment of ash of <s>rasa</s>.
In a low, broad, square pit two hastas across,
filled with a thousand forest cow-dung cakes, the medicine to be fired,
carefully sealed in a krauñcī vessel, should be placed on top of the lump.
Half a thousand forest cow-dung cakes should be arranged above the krauñcī vessel.
One should kindle the fire there; this is remembered as the mahāpuṭa.
A puṭa of the measure of an elephant's cubit is remembered as the gajapuṭa.
Some say that the gajapuṭa is a puṭa above and below of the measure of an elephant.
A square pit of the measure of an elephant's cubit
should be filled with giriṇḍa cakes amounting to half the former quantity of cow dung.
This is called the gajapuṭa, producing great efficacy.

children.text: itthaṃ cāratnike kuṇḍe puṭaṃ vārāhapuṭam ucyate ||
children.translated_text: Thus, in a pit of one aratni, the puṭa is called the vārāhapuṭa.
Then one should arrange it up to the neck, filled with upalaśāṭhī cakes.
There one should place a jar filled with the substance to be fired.
A crucible containing <s>rasa</s>, with all its parts covered in sand, in a pit,
should be covered with blazing cow-dung cakes; that apparatus is called bhūdhara.
Here, when the fire has been properly buried in the earth two aṅgulas below,
and a puṭa is above it, that puṭa is called bhūdhara.

children.text: tathā cānyad yantraṃ rasendracintāmaṇau hastaikapramāṇamātrabhūgarbhāntarnikhātāṃ prāgvatkācaghaṭīṃ nāticipiṭamukhīṃ nātyucchūnamukhīṃ maṣībhājanaprāyāṃ karparacakrikayā kācacakrikayā vā niruddhavadanavivarāṃ mṛnmayīṃ vā vidhāya karīṣairupari puṭo deya ityanyadyantram
children.translated_text: And there is another apparatus in the <s>Rasendracintāmaṇi</s>: a glass flask, buried underground to the measure of one hasta as before, with a mouth neither too flat nor too swollen, like an ink-vessel, its mouth-opening closed with a potsherd disk or a glass disk, or else made of clay, is to receive a puṭa above with cow dung; this is another apparatus.
According to <s>Trilocana</s>, it is to be done with an iron container made of two unequal pieces, within a sand apparatus, or else in a bhūdhara.
A large vessel filled with husks, with a crucible containing <s>rasa</s> in the middle,

children.text: vahninā vihite pāke tad bhāṇḍapuṭam ucyate ||
children.translated_text: when cooked by fire, is called the vessel-puṭa.
These are to be understood everywhere in the case of iron and the like.
But when the measure of the puṭa has not been stated, the strength and weakness of the substance to be accomplished
should be understood, and the puṭa should be given by those skilled in reasoning by supposition and exclusion.

children.text: etāni puṭāni yatra yatropayuktāni tatra tatra vicārya deyāni
children.translated_text: Wherever these puṭas are useful, there they should be applied after due consideration.
The first puṭa is only with cow dung.

children.text: dvitīyādipuṭe punargandhaṃ dattvā nimbūrasena mardayitvā kukkuṭapuṭaṃ dadyāt
children.translated_text: On the second and subsequent puṭas, after again adding sulphur, grinding it with lemon juice, he should give a kukkuṭa-puṭa heating.
He should do this until the prescribed number of puṭa heatings has been completed.
This is to be understood everywhere in the killing of iron and the other metals.

children.text: yadi tu tīkṣṇādilohamāraṇaṃ tadā gajapuṭāni jñeyāni tathā tāmrādimāraṇe kāṣṭhādijanyo'gnipāko jñeyaḥ
children.translated_text: But if it is the killing of sharp iron and similar metals, gaja-puṭas are to be understood; likewise, in the killing of copper and the like, cooking by fire produced from wood and so on is to be understood.
Thus, the distinctions among puṭa heatings.
The lord of sages, <s>Nāgārjuna</s>, taught the science of metals, which is exceedingly profound.
For the recollection of that meaning, we state this in clear syllables.

children.text: śītodakaṃ payaḥ kṣaudraṃ sarpir ityekaśo dviśaḥ
children.translated_text: Cold water, milk, honey, and ghee, singly, in pairs,
or in threes, or all together: after first preparing it, one should set it aside again.

children.text: mene muniḥ svatantre yaḥ pākaṃ na palapañcakād arvāk
children.translated_text: The sage held in his own treatise that the cooking should not be less than five palas,
nor above thirteen palas, because of the fault of excessive labor.
There, when iron is to be cooked, beginning with five palas and up to thirteen palas of kānta iron,

children.text: lohāt triguṇā triphalā grāhyā ṣaḍbhiḥ palair adhikā ||
children.translated_text: triphala should be taken in three times the amount of the metal, increased by six palas.
The killing, puṭa-heating, and vessel-cooking are to be accomplished with one part of triphala;
two parts of triphala are to be taken for the cooking of iron.
Everywhere, for one part intended for puṭa-heating and the like of iron, the number is eight śarāvas,
and for each pala, water three times as much is to be taken for making the decoction.
For the portion beginning with seven palas and ending with fifteen, with śarāvas of water,
the water should be made greater by three up to eleven, respectively.

children.text: tatrāṣṭamastu bhāgaḥ śeṣaḥ kvāthasya yatnataḥ sthāpyaḥ
children.translated_text: There the eighth part should be carefully kept as the remainder of the decoction;
for with that the killing, puṭa-heating, and vessel-cooking will be accomplished.
But for cooking, when there are two parts of triphala, the water should equal the number of śarāvas,
pala by pala, increased by two śarāvas.

children.text: tatra caturtho bhāgaḥ śeṣo nipuṇaiḥ prayatnato grāhyaḥ
children.translated_text: There the fourth part, as the remainder, should be carefully taken by the skilled;

children.text: ayasaḥ pākārthatvāt sa ca sarvasmāt pradhānatamaḥ ||
children.translated_text: because it is for the cooking of iron, and that is the most important of all.
For cooking aśmasāra, beginning with five palas and ending with thirteen palas,
there should be two śarāvas of milk, increased by quarter-measures and by one half.
The measure begins with five palas; in its absence, it should be taken in accordance with that proportion.
Beginning with four, certainly, and, if possible, more than thirteen.
Powders of triphalā, trikaṭu, citraka, kānta, krāmaka, and viḍaṅga,
and of nutmeg, mace, cardamom, kaṅkola, and cloves,
and also powders of white and black cumin should be equal in amount to the iron.
Triphalā, trikaṭu, and viḍaṅga are fixed; the others are according to constitution.
Those born from the head, black like collyrium, are considered proper in the rasāyana procedure.
And accordingly:
Bodies on this earth are chiefly of kapha, pitta, and wind;
there the fallen demons, and the regions too, are of that same kind.
From them arose mountain-essences, superior, inferior, and middling.
The field of kapha is the place of the head; the heart is the vessel of pitta;

children.text: vāyo nābhir adhaḥ kṣetramiti dehavido viduḥ
children.translated_text: the region below the navel belongs to wind: so knowers of the body know.
Those born from the chest are for destroying disease; those born from kapha are for enema treatment;
those born from the head are for bodily perfection. Thus they are considered threefold.

children.text: śirojā iti bhūpatitadānavaśiraḥprajātā lauhāḥ kajjalābhā bhavanti
children.translated_text: 'Born from the head' means that irons produced from the heads of demons fallen on the earth are black like collyrium.
The meaning is that these very ones are to be taken for the sake of rasāyana.
When the defects of black iron have been destroyed by nutmeg and the other substances, by clove and kānta,
of that,
in proportion to the attainment of kṣepra, and in proportion to all attainment of kṣepra, and for what is deficient, with one and the other measures. [Text corrupt.]
A single kānta-krāmaka removes completely every defect of iron.
Ghee should be taken in double, triple, or quadruple quantity, according to constitution.

children.text: yadi bheṣajabhūyastvaṃ stokatvaṃ vā tathāpi cūrṇānām
children.translated_text: If the medicines are abundant, or if the powders are scanty, even so,
their numerical equality with the iron becomes greater or smaller according as they are more or less.
Now the complete procedure for loading kānta and the other irons is being stated.

children.text: yasya kṛte tallauhaṃ paktavyaṃ tasya śubhadivase
children.translated_text: For the person for whose sake that iron is to be cooked, on an auspicious day for him,
on a piece of ground made beautiful with mṛdaṅga, raṅga, and other decorations, after fully worshipping <s>Śiva</s>,
having established the fire according to the altar rite and offered oblations there,
thus, according to the metal, by adapting the respectively stated medicine,
everywhere the adjustment of the respectively stated medicine is to be made.
Above and below one should place viḍa, in the amount of one eighth of the rasendra.
One should not take less or more; otherwise it would cause a defect.
The medicine which is given above and below by the wise for purification,
that receives the designation viḍa: this has been explained.

children.text: ṣaṭtruṭyaścaikalikṣā syāt ṣaḍlikṣā yūka eva ca
children.translated_text: Six truṭis make one likṣā, and six likṣās make one yūka;
six yūkas are called one rajas; this has been stated for you, good-vowed one.

children.text: ṣaḍrajaḥ sarṣapaḥ sākṣātsiddhārthaḥ sa ca kīrtitaḥ
children.translated_text: Six rajas are exactly one mustard seed, and that is called siddhārtha;
six siddhārthas, O goddess, are declared to be one barley grain.
With six barley grains there is one guñjā, and six guñjās make one māṣaka;

children.text: māṣā dvādaśa tolaḥ syāt taccaturthiḥ palaṃ bhavet ||
children.translated_text: twelve māṣas make one tola, and four of those make one pala.
Thirty-two palas, goddess, are declared to be one śubha;

children.text: śubhasya tu sahasre dve bhāra ekaḥ prakīrtitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: and two thousand śubhas are declared to be one bhāra.
Weights are various, light and heavy, in weighing;
the standard weight is equal to a mānasa and is fashioned from iron, silver, and the like.
The sequence up to the rājikā and maṇa is to be known by the wise;
and the retanī is just a span; the chinnaka, eight aṅgulas, is auspicious.
The tongs should be made in two forms, the parrot-beak and the crow-beak.
The long gripping tongs should be one hasta in measure and very handsome.
The scissors should be shaped like the blossom of unmattā, both light and heavy.
For cutting metals, the cutter should be auspicious and eight aṅgulas long.
The kāṇa, two hastas in measure, is useful for stirring metals.

children.text: dvividhā hariṇī kāryā laghuḥ sthūlā ca śobhanā ||
children.translated_text: The hariṇī should be made in two forms, light and heavy, and attractive.

children.text: hastāḍī dvimukhī kāryā yantrākārā ca vartulā
children.translated_text: The hastāḍī should be made double-mouthed, apparatus-shaped, and round.
With two, four, eight, five, and also ten mouths,

children.text: prakartavyā ghanā bhavyā dhātūnāṃ kuṭṭane hitā
children.translated_text: a solid and excellent one should be made, useful for pounding metals.
Crucibles and pans are of many kinds, made of iron, udumbara wood, or clay.
Likewise bowls should be known, and glass ones, like cups.
Pestles, mortars, and the like should be made of firm wood or good iron.
For determining the color of gold and the other metals, the touchstone has been described.
The varālaka, the pāhara, the kuśikuddali, and the vardhana are also taught.

children.text: bījasādhane gaganaṃ jārayevādau ityādivakṣyamāṇakramād abhrakagandhamākṣikādisattvapiṣṭikā nirūpyante
children.translated_text: In preparing the seed, first one should digest gagana, and so on: according to the sequence to be stated, the piṣṭikās of the essences of mica, sulphur, māksika, and the like are explained.

children.text: tatra vyomno daśaguṇaṃ sattvaṃ sattvāddaśaguṇā drutiḥ iti vyomacūrṇasattvadrutiṣu tāvaccūrṇarūpāṃ piṣṭiṃ nirūpayati
children.translated_text: Here, since the essence from vyoman is ten times the vyoman, and the druti is ten times the essence, he first explains, among the powder, essence, and druti of vyoman, the piṣṭi that has the form of powder.
The making of vyoman-piṣṭi, in the <s>Rasārṇava</s>:
Vyoman treated with alkaline and sour substances and with the first rajas,
triturated with the water-particles of the three creations and with tumburu juice,
digested or else heated in a puṭa, and with the juice of yavaciñcā,
with śatāvarī, guhā, rambhā, meghanāda, and punarnavā,

children.text: śigruko yavaciñcā ca bhāvitaṃ tadrasaiḥ kramāt
children.translated_text: and with śigru and yavaciñcā, is to be treated successively with their juices.
The white root of Umā, and the root of Kauberī as well,
kadalī, musalī, śigru, tāmbūlī, bāṇa, and pīluka,
alambuṣā, balā, kolī, āsphoṭā, and kharamañjarī,
tumburu and bitter greens: with the single juice of one of these,
mica mixed with rājikā and vyoṣa should be steamed for three days.
With kāśīśa, tumburu, salt, borax, and alkali joined together,
and by the previously taught abhiṣava procedure, mercury moves at once.

children.text: atra prathamena rajasā pūrvoktenābhiṣekeṇa sṛṣṭitrayaṃ lavaṇatrayam umātasī kauberī uttaravāruṇī yavaciñcā tintiḍī
children.translated_text: Here 'with the first rajas' means with the previously stated sprinkling; 'the three creations' means the three salts; Umā is atasī, Kauberī is uttaravāruṇī, and yavaciñcā is tintiḍī.
This is the meaning: a piṣṭi should be made with the juice of yavaciñcā from material triturated with alkaline and sour substances and heated in a puṭa.
